subtype: Approach: learning from a past drawdown [Revision]
passage:
The deadline to change the fund mix was three o'clock, and Sudha had two hours and a slow internet line. Yogesh, at the next desk, leaned across. "Did you sell?"
"No." Sudha pulled out a notebook from two years back, the pages soft at the corners. Last time a smaller fall had scared her, and she had waited, and it had come back within months. But her own note said something else too: "Too much in one risky sector. I felt sick every day."
"So you're doing nothing again?"
"Nothing except this." Sudha moved a small part out of that sector before the window closed and kept the rest as planned.
Then Sudha closed the laptop and took a breath.

qa.q: What time was the deadline to change the fund mix?
What was Sudha feeling in the notebook entry from two years ago?
qa.a: Sudha felt sick and scared about the risky sector, as the note itself says.

qa.q: What could Sudha do if the risky sector recovers before the next review?
qa.a: Sudha could leave the smaller share as it is and review it at the planned time, not chase the recovery.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have seen Sudha's choice?
qa.a: Yogesh seemed unsure, asking if Sudha was doing nothing again, though the small move shows a plan behind the calm.

grounding: The passage shows an investor who recalls a smaller earlier fall that recovered, reads past notes and sticks with the plan while lowering exposure to one risky sector.

subtype: Approach: learning from a past drawdown [Revision]
passage:
When the market fell twenty percent in October, Leela felt the old panic rising in her Hyderabad flat. Then she remembered: two years ago it had fallen twelve percent, and she had written notes.
She found the file on her laptop. "Date: March. Down 12%. Felt like selling everything. Didn't. Recovered by September." And underneath, in capitals: "MY TECH FUND FELL TWICE AS MUCH AS EVERYTHING ELSE. I DIDN'T KNOW I HAD SO MUCH IN ONE SECTOR."
She read it twice. The first part told her to stay with the plan. The second told her what to change. She checked: tech was again nearly half her portfolio. That evening she called her friend Nilesh, who had studied finance, to talk it through, and booked a session with a registered adviser. She kept her monthly plan running, and after the adviser meeting she moved part of the tech fund into a broader fund.
In her notes she added a new line: "October. Down 20%. Stayed. Spread out."

qa.q: What did Leela's old notes say about her tech fund?
qa.a: That it fell twice as much as everything else, and that she hadn't known she had so much in one sector.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when the market fell in October?
qa.a: Leela felt the old panic rising, until her notes steadied her.

qa.q: What made Leela's response balanced rather than all-or-nothing?
qa.a: She kept the monthly plan running but reduced the one risky sector, after talking to Nilesh and a registered adviser.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see Leela's call?
qa.a: Nilesh likely sees a friend thinking carefully rather than panicking, and is glad to help her talk it through.

grounding: It shows an investor recalling an earlier smaller fall, rereading notes from then, staying with the plan and reducing exposure to one risky sector.

passage:
"You're not selling?" Imran stared at Hrithik's screen. "You're down eighteen percent!"
"I was down eleven two years ago too. Look." Hrithik opened a note. "I wrote this then: 'Wanted to sell. Didn't. Back to normal in seven months.'"
"So you're just ignoring it?"
"No. Scroll down."
Imran read aloud: "'Next time, check how much is in small companies. They fell hardest.'"
"Right. So this morning I checked. Almost forty percent of my money is in one small-company fund. That's too much for me."
"So you'll sell that?"
"Not all of it, and not today in a panic. I've booked a call with the adviser on Friday to talk about bringing it down. The rest of the plan stays the same. My monthly amount still goes in on the tenth."
"You're strangely calm."
"Past me left instructions."

qa.q: How much of Hrithik's money was in one small-company fund?
Why is Hrithik calm while Imran is alarmed?
qa.a: Hrithik has notes from the last fall showing it recovered, so Hrithik feels steadier and knows what to adjust.
The monthly amount keeps going, as the notes suggest, while the one risky fund will be reduced after talking to the adviser, not in a panic.

qa.q: How does Imran see Hrithik's decision at first?
qa.a: Imran thinks Hrithik is ignoring a big loss and finds the calm strange.

grounding: It shows an investor rereading notes from an earlier recovered fall, sticking with the plan but planning to reduce exposure to one risky fund.
